ops.title: Cardinality — read the line in both directions

cells.c-test: One X has how many Y? Then: one Y has how many X? The pair of answers is the cardinality.
cells.c-seen: Every example in the class is worked this way.

cells.c-test: One customer has one user ID; one user ID belongs to one customer.
cells.c-seen: Almost never between tables — if two columns map one to one, they live in the same table.

cells.c-test: One brand has many products; one product belongs to exactly one brand.
cells.c-notation: Bar on the one side, crow's foot on the many side
cells.c-keys: Primary key to foreign key — the repeating side is the foreign key
cells.c-seen: Everywhere. This is the one you actually work with.

cells.c-test: One book is written by several authors; one author writes many books.
cells.c-keys: No shared column can hold it
cells.c-seen: Never drawn as a line. A column holds one value per row, so the list has nowhere to live.

cells.c-rel: Junction table — how many-to-many is really stored
cells.c-test: One customer has many purchase rows, one purchase row has one customer; and the same read from the product side.
cells.c-notation: Two one-to-many lines meeting at a middle table
cells.c-keys: Foreign keys to both parents, no primary key of its own
cells.c-seen: customer_purchases is exactly this shape. The many-to-many survives as a path, not a line.

cells.c-rel: Which level is the relationship at?
cells.c-test: Table level, always — the E in ER is entity, and an entity is a table.
cells.c-keys: Executed through a column (customer_id here, customer_id there)
cells.c-seen: The distinction that answers most cardinality doubts.

ops.title: DQL — the clauses you actually get

ops.label: DQL — see and extract, change nothing
ops.detail: About 80% of the course. You can display and download; you cannot alter a single value in the table. The analogy is view access to a spreadsheet — the download is yours, the table is untouched.

ops.label: Why you only get DQL
ops.detail: The framing question: will you be given access to edit production tables? No — and the taxonomy of sublanguages falls out of that answer.

ops.label: DDL changes the table's structure — ALTER, DROP, add or rename a column
ops.detail: Run by SQL developers. With DROP TABLE you would have a one-command exit from a notice period.

ops.label: DML changes the data inside it — UPDATE, INSERT, DELETE
ops.detail: Structure versus data is the line the instructor keeps returning to. If everyone can update the sales records, nobody can trust the sales records.

ops.label: DCL grants and revokes access — GRANT, REVOKE
ops.detail: The DBA's job. The DBA decides who gets which sublanguage.

ops.label: TCL is the approval gate — COMMIT, ROLLBACK
ops.detail: A DROP does not go live when it is typed. Someone must COMMIT it and someone must approve that commit, so important tables are not dropped by accident. ROLLBACK is the undo.

ops.label: SELECT names the columns — * means all of them
Columns you do not name are not displayed, not deleted
ops.detail: The same fact as DQL being view-only, arriving from a different direction. Nothing changed in the back end. It is tested twice more, on AS and on the inline calculation.

ops.label: SELECT *, adds one more column to all of them
ops.detail: The comma after the star is the whole trick. The new column lands at the end because the star came first; reverse them and it lands first. To place it in the middle there is no shortcut — write out every column name in the order you want.

ops.label: FROM names the table, written dataset.table
ops.detail: Wrapped in backticks. The dataset prefix was called optional but cumbersome; every query in the class writes it out in full.

ops.label: ORDER BY sorts — ascending unless you write DESC
ops.detail: It needs a column name; ORDER BY on its own will not run. Text sorts alphabetically, A to Z being the ascending direction. DESC is compulsory if you want descending; ASC never is.

ops.label: Several columns: left to right is priority
ops.detail: The first column sorts first; the second only breaks ties inside it. Swapping the two changes the answer.

ops.label: Direction attaches per column, so directions can mix
ops.detail: ORDER BY product_category_id DESC, product_name — category descending, then name ascending within each category.

ops.label: LIMIT n returns at most n rows — rows only, never columns
ops.detail: The problem it solves: SELECT * on a billion-row table makes you wait a long time just to see what is inside. There is no TOP keyword in BigQuery.

ops.label: OFFSET n skips n rows — positional, never conditional
ops.detail: It counts; it does not evaluate. Written after LIMIT, and LIMIT is compulsory for OFFSET to run — LIMIT works fine on its own. Skipping a row identified by a condition is a window function, later in the course.

ops.label: Ties are settled by processing order, not by your query
ops.detail: ORDER BY runs before OFFSET, so the sort decides what position one is. Where rows tie, the sort has said all it has to say and the engine orders them however it processed them. Identical rows make this invisible; rows differing in other columns make the result unstable. The fix is to keep adding sort columns until the sort cannot tie — which is what transaction_time is doing in the worked example.

ops.label: Inline calculation — arithmetic between columns, one row at a time
ops.detail: All four operators work. Every row is computed independently, the way a spreadsheet formula fills down. The result is displayed, never stored.

ops.label: AS names an output column — any column, not only computed ones
ops.detail: The header changes, the back end does not. Without an alias BigQuery labels a computed column f0_, which is unusable output — that is the motivation for AS.

ops.label: ROUND(value, decimals) — the second argument is optional
ops.detail: Omit it and you get zero decimal places: ROUND(39.5) is 40. ROUND(39.93, 1) is 39.9; ROUND(39.96, 1) is 40.0. ROUND is a function — it acts on a value — as against a clause, which is structural.

ops.label: CEIL and FLOOR exist — nearest integer up, nearest integer down
ops.detail: Named but not taught. Set as homework: try them in Excel and in a SELECT.

ops.markdown:
**Backtick, not single quote.** The character wrapping `` `farmers_market.product` `` is the key left of the `1`, above Tab. Unshifted it gives the backtick; shifted it gives the tilde `~` — which is the name used throughout the class, and it is the wrong one.

The difference is not cosmetic. Backticks wrap an **identifier** — the name of a thing in the database. Single quotes wrap a **string literal** — a piece of text data, like `'P1'` in a WHERE clause. So `FROM 'farmers_market.product'` is not a near miss the parser can guess through; it says "select from the text value farmers_market.product", and a text value is not a table. That is exactly what comes back:

```
Syntax error: Unexpected string literal 'farmers_market.product' at [1:15]
```

Read it as "you handed me a string where a table name goes" and it diagnoses itself. This is the most common error of the class.

**The semicolon is a full stop.** Not required for a single statement. Required when several run together — it is the only way SQL knows where one ends and the next begins. Skip it and you get `Expected end of input but got keyword SELECT`. So always write it.

**Run one statement out of many** by selecting that text and clicking Run. This is also the fix for the error above.

**Case and whitespace do not matter.** `select` and `SELECT` are identical, and indentation is irrelevant in SQL, unlike other languages. The style note attached: do not be miserly with spaces.

**Comments:** `--` and `#` both work.

**The smoke test for the setup:** `SELECT * FROM \`farmers_market.product\`;` should return **23 rows**. Also given in class: 28 rows in `customer`, 1003 in `customer_purchases`.

**Identifier spellings here are transcript-derived.** No class-notes PDF exists for this lecture, so `product` against `products` and `customer` against `customers` are unresolved, and `cost_to_customer_per_qty` was never spelled out aloud. Verify each one in the BigQuery panel before running a query verbatim — the same procedure already boarded on the filtering board.

ops.title: What the quizzes caught, and what was mis-named

ops.markdown:
**The four quiz points.**

1. Brand to phone models is **one-to-many** — one brand has many models, one model belongs to exactly one brand.
2. **`DESC` is compulsory if you want descending; `ASC` is not**, because ascending is the default.
3. LIMIT and OFFSET, four true/false statements. True: OFFSET skips the top n rows, and LIMIT decides how many rows display. False: LIMIT skips rows, and OFFSET decides how many display. Flagged in class as the one to read slowly.
4. **`AS` can rename any column, not only computed ones.** By the instructor's read-out about 30% of the class answered otherwise, which is why the point is made three times in the lecture.

**Named wrongly in class, and worth recognising both ways.**

- The **backtick** is called a tilde throughout. The instruction is right, the name is not.
- A **candidate key** is defined as a combination of columns that is jointly unique and not null. That is a **composite** key; a candidate key is any column or set that could serve as the primary key. Carried over from session 1.
- **"Relationships, also known as schemas."** A schema is the structure of a database, not a synonym for a relationship.
- Asked how many relationship types there are, the answer given is three — **omitting many-to-many**, which the same session had just taught at length. A slip in a fast reply, not a correction to the lesson.
- **`DESC`** is called first a function and then an attribute. It is neither: it is a sort-direction keyword. The clause / function / attribute split is a teaching device rather than standard taxonomy — the behaviour taught is correct throughout.

**Stated without support, so do not carry it forward.** That `ROUND(100)` always returns a decimal — return type follows input type. That Snowflake holds almost a monopoly in warehouses. That BigQuery is "neither a database nor a warehouse, just a platform" — it is generally described as a warehouse, and Scaler's own revision notes do not repeat the claim. That the dataset is a business by Amazon Fresh — a useful mental model for the schema, not background about the data.

**Two things left open.** The expected first-row values for the most-recent-transactions query are garbled in the recording and are not reconstructed anywhere — check against your own output. And what happens when OFFSET exceeds the row count was asked and never answered; the reply addresses only OFFSET being larger than LIMIT. Worth putting to the instructor.

**Scaler's auto-notes list `WHERE` among this class's commands. It was not taught here** — it appears once as a bare name in a list of clauses. Filtering is the next lecture.
